items.title: The Verifiable Action Card: Trustworthy Human-in-the-Loop Control for Secure Autonomous Agents
items.one_liner: The Verifiable Action Card architectural defense stops browser agent prompt injections by binding user approval to ground-truth actions.
items.summary: Researchers introduced the Verifiable Action Card (VAC), an architectural defense designed to protect agentic browsers against indirect prompt injection, deceptive confirmation interfaces, and confused-deputy attacks. VAC reconstructs approval information directly from ground-truth pending browser actions and trusted intent provenance, rendering out-of-band confirmations in the trusted browser chrome while binding user approval to the exact dispatched action. Evaluated across 24 scenarios, VAC reduced attack success rates from 68%–100% down to 0% across multiple LLMs without increasing false-block rates or degrading legitimate task completion.
items.bottom_line: The Verifiable Action Card provides a secure human-in-the-loop mechanism that completely neutralizes indirect prompt injection attacks in agentic browsers.

items.title: Safety Does Not Compose: Non-Decaying Loop State for Autonomous LLM Agents
items.one_liner: LoopHarness maintains a non-decaying persistent safety state to block multi-step attacks in autonomous LLM agent loops.
items.summary: Researchers demonstrate that safety safeguards for autonomous LLM agents fail to compose across multiple iterations, leaving trajectory-scoped monitors vulnerable to multi-step attacks where evidence is fragmented. While a geometrically decaying risk score is insufficient to stop persistent adversaries, the authors present LoopHarness, a loop-level framework providing non-decaying persistent safety state. Under mediated commits and an arbiter detection floor, LoopHarness bounds unauthorized irreversible actions to a constant value independent of horizon length $N$.
items.bottom_line: Session-scoped LLM safety monitors fail against multi-iteration fragmented attacks unless state persistence is enforced at the loop level.

items.title: ASLEval: Measuring Privacy Exposure Displacement in LLM Agent Sessions
items.one_liner: ASLEval benchmark reveals that traditional proxy metrics miss nearly half of privacy exposures in LLM agent sessions.
items.summary: Researchers introduce ASLEval, an authorization-aware framework designed to measure privacy exposure displacement in tool-using LLM agent sessions. The tool pre-registers a hidden target set and evaluates all visible exits while tracking internal evidence traces. Evaluations across enterprise-style runtimes show that expected-outlet-only views miss 46.9% of actual exposure, and attacker self-reports combine omissions with high false discovery rates. The findings demonstrate the necessity of benchmarking complete visible boundaries alongside task utility.
items.bottom_line: Evaluating LLM agent privacy requires tracking complete visible session boundaries rather than relying on local action proxies.
